newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch dilemma on how to combat rival soccer gangs.
newsitem.headline: Dutch dilemma on how to combat rival soccer gangs.

text.p: The hatred between rival Dutch soccer gangs is just as intense, but the battleground for their brief but brutal confrontations has changed since the 1970s when fans invaded pitches and fought on crumbling concrete terraces.

The death of an Ajax Amsterdam gang leader, a 35-year-old hotel owner, in violent clashes with rival Feyenoord Rotterdam supporters on waste ground near a motorway on Sunday marks a turning point for this small, soccer-crazed country.
It was the first fatality linked to the soccer hooliganism that has blighted the sport for over 20 years.
The Netherlands, in common with most countries riddled with the hooliganism disease, thought it had wrested control from the thugs who terrorised soccer crowds in the 1970s and 1980s.

But, while better policing and the move to all-seater stadiums appeared to have rid the game of its worst excesses of violence, the brief calm has prompted a new generation of hooligans hell-bent on carrying on the age-old rivalries.

Owing more to the gang warfare of the United States than to the traditional European image of pitched battles between fans and riot police, the new breed of hooligan is more sophisticated and organised, the fighting pre-arranged and premeditated.

Today's gangs, a volatile mix of old-style, street-hard skinhead and modish, professional thirtysomething, have taken their brutal skirmishing away from the soccer grounds and heavy policing presence to the urban wastelands and motorway parks.
Meetings are pre-arranged by mobile telephone, allowing the organisers to change venue at the last minute.

The fans, wearing jeans, jackets and often balaclavas, arrive by car, brandishing all manner of weapons, but nearly always knives and baseball bats, go into brief combat and then disperse at the sound of police sirens.

While these gangs swear allegiance to soccer clubs and wear their teams' colours and insignia -- many die-hard Feyenoord fans sport an "SCF" (Sporting Club Feyenoord) tattoo -- the sport itself claims it is powerless to intervene.
Clubs have traditionally been held culpable for violence by their fans. But many now reckon that this latest gang-style feuding has little to do with the game.

"I have said it many times before and say it again now...this (violence) has nothing to do with football," Feyenoord chairman Jorien van den Herik said. "Fighting of this sort falls outside the competence of the clubs and the (Dutch) soccer association."
"This is pure criminality. Football is just an excuse," state secretary for sport Erica Terpstra said on Sunday.
Deputy Prime Minister Hans Dijkstal said the government was losing its grip in the face of escalating violence.

"These are gangs of hardened criminals, groups who seek each other out to fight," he said. Calling for tougher sentences, he added: "This is hard work for the police and judiciary. We must track down these groups and punish them."
Politicians, meeting police and soccer chiefs for urgent talks on Monday, remain divided over how to react.

The conservative Liberal Party, the rightist element in the ruling three-party coalition, has called for maximum penalties to deter these "small mobile armies" from staging their brutal combat in public places.
The senior coalition partner Labour Party prefers to improve police infiltration in the gangs, keeping mobile troops up-to-date with the gangs' last-minute venue alterations.

The police, working with the criminal intelligence agency set up in the 1980s to track soccer hooligans, knew in advance that the rival gangs had set up a meeting, but were powerless to stop it when the venue was switched at the last moment.
"We tried everything...to keep the two gangs apart, but we would have needed airborne troops to get between them," said local Kennemerland chief of police Bob Visser.

There is a long history of rivalry between Feyenoord and Ajax, bordering on naked hatred which, in part, reflects the cultural divide between the nation's two largest cities. Rotterdam, the industrial heart, has long felt slighted by aristocratic Amsterdam.
In October 1989, 14 people were injured when a Feyenoord supporter lobbed a home-made bomb in amongst Ajax fans during a league game in Amsterdam.

And last November fans hurled fire-bombs and pelted police with ball bearings ahead of a league game in Rotterdam. At the ground, over 100 baying Feyenoord supporters attacked the Ajax team coach, hurling bottles and stones and breaking windows.
Dutch media have dubbed games between these two teams, among the most successful in the Netherlands, as "The Match of Hate".
